power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Purpose: To develop and validate a fully automated pipeline that measures skeletal muscle and adipose tissue at L1 and L3 on routine CT with varied scan ranges, slice orders and contrast phases, rejects levels outside the scan and converts measures to non-contrast equivalents.

The pipeline (sarco) combines orientation detection, L1/L3 localisation with out-of-range rejection, U-Net segmentation, six-class contrast-phase estimation, phase-specific conversion to non-contrast-equivalent values and, as an auxiliary output, muscle and marrow age estimation.

We evaluated it on five single-centre datasets (4986 series): agreement with radiologist-corrected labels using five-fold cross-fitting (2025 series), artificially truncated scans, contrast-enhanced series paired with non-contrast series of the same examination, and the prognostic value of fully automated measures in 2006 patients after curative cancer surgery.
TotalSegmentator served as a comparator.
Results: On held-out folds, L3 skeletal muscle area (SMA) agreed with the reference (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.983; bias +1.35 cm²).
On truncated scans processed with cross-fitted localisation 1.

Body composition measured on CT, in particular the skeletal muscle area (SMA) and mean skeletal muscle density (MSMD) at the third lumbar vertebra (L3), is associated with outcomes in many cancers and is increasingly used as an opportunistic imaging biomarker [1] [2] [3].

text.text: In our institution, low muscle mass on preoperative CT was associated with cancer-specific and overall survival after curative surgery for gastrointestinal and urological cancers [4], and low muscle attenuation with overall survival in the same cohort [5].

text.text: Manual or semi-automatic measurement is, however, time-consuming.
Several deep-learning tools now segment muscle and adipose tissue on CT, including the widely used open-source TotalSegmentator [6].
text.formatted: Several deep-learning tools now segment muscle and adipose tissue on CT, including the widely used open-source TotalSegmentator <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Three practical problems remain.

First, most tools assume that the target vertebral level is within the scan; studies of automatic L3 selection have often excluded examinations in which L3 was not imaged [7], so the behaviour of these tools on short scans, such as upperabdominal dynamic CT, is largely unknown.

text.text: Second, the chosen slice affects the measured area [8], so comparisons between tools are confounded by different slice definitions.

text.text: Third, iodinated contrast medium increases muscle attenuation by a few to more than 10 Hounsfield units (HU) depending on the phase [9] [10] [11] [12], whereas published attenuation thresholds were derived from non-contrast CT [13], and existing corrections were derived for a single phase [10] or apply one phase-independent offset [14]; neither estimates the phase from the image.

text.text: We developed sarco, a pipeline that runs as a plug-in of the CIRCUS research platform [15].
text.formatted: We developed sarco, a pipeline that runs as a plug-in of the CIRCUS research platform <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: It detects the slice order, localises L1 and L3 or reports that they are out of range, segments muscle and vertebral bone, estimates the contrast phase from the image and converts measures to non-contrast (phase 0) equivalents.

As auxiliary outputs, it also estimates muscle and marrow age, height and weight; these are summarised in the Online Resource, and the focus of this study is robustness to scan range, slice order and contrast phase.

We evaluated (1) its robustness to slice order and truncated scans; (2) its agreement with radiologist-corrected labels, using cross-fitting; (3) phase estimation and phase-0 conversion against same-examination non-contrast series; and (4) whether its fully automated measures reproduce published prognostic associations.
TotalSegmentator was used as a comparator where its outputs were comparable.

The primary prognostic comparisons were specified in writing on 22 October 2026, before the cross-fitted, fully automated analysis was run, but after exploratory analyses of the same cohort with the reference labels; the study was not pre-registered.

text.text: Five datasets of CT examinations performed at The University of Tokyo Hospital were used (Table 1).
text.formatted: Five datasets of CT examinations performed at The University of Tokyo Hospital were used (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: All images were pseudonymised (patient identifiers replaced by study codes) and converted to NIfTI; the slice thickness equalled the slice interval in all series.
Sample sizes were determined by the available data; no power calculation was performed.

• Dataset main (2039 patients, one preoperative series each; CT from 2005-2018): patients who underwent curative surgery for gastric, oesophageal, renal or urothelial cancer; 2015 of them were previously reported [4, 5].
text.formatted: • Dataset main (2039 patients, one preoperative series each; CT from 2005-2018): patients who underwent curative surgery for gastric, oesophageal, renal or urothelial cancer; 2015 of them were previously reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref>.

text.text: L1 and L3 labels of skeletal muscle and vertebral cortical and medullary bone were available (see Reference labels), together with measured height and weight and outcomes.

• Dataset L (321 patients, 1675 series, 2022): multiphase abdominal CT acquired with a fixed protocol of non-contrast, early arterial, late arterial, portal venous and equilibrium phases; 203 of these examinations were previously reported [9].
text.formatted: • Dataset L (321 patients, 1675 series, 2022): multiphase abdominal CT acquired with a fixed protocol of non-contrast, early arterial, late arterial, portal venous and equilibrium phases; 203 of these examinations were previously reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: • Dataset P (99 patients, 222 series, 2025): pancreatobiliary dynamic CT with non-contrast, venous and equilibrium phases.
• Dataset HC (474 patients, 474 series, 2007-2008): whole-body non-contrast CT from healthscreening positron emission tomography/CT.
• Dataset O (144 patients, 576 series, 2025): other clinical CT with various phases and scan ranges, including head and neck, chest and abdominal examinations.
Datasets P, HC and O have not been reported previously.

The reference phase was defined by the protocol in Dataset L, was non-contrast in all of Dataset HC, and was taken from the DICOM series description and the protocol name in the radiology information system in Datasets P and O. A few patients appeared in more than one dataset (Online Resource, Fig. S2).
text.formatted: The reference phase was defined by the protocol in Dataset L, was non-contrast in all of Dataset HC, and was taken from the DICOM series description and the protocol name in the radiology information system in Datasets P and O. A few patients appeared in more than one dataset (Online Resource, Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S2</ref>).

text.text: Scanners from five vendors were used (Online Resource, Table S2).
text.formatted: Scanners from five vendors were used (Online Resource, Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: Reference labels in Dataset main were produced as previously described [4, 18]: a first version of the segmentation model was trained on manually painted cases (ITK-SNAP [19]), applied to all cases in CIRCUS, and its output was corrected by radiologists.
text.formatted: Reference labels in Dataset main were produced as previously described <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18]</ref>: a first version of the segmentation model was trained on manually painted cases (ITK-SNAP <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>), applied to all cases in CIRCUS, and its output was corrected by radiologists.

text.text: The reference slice for each level was the slice on which both transverse processes were visible.
Because the reference labels originate from an earlier version of the same model family, agreement may favour the proposed pipeline over other tools.
The pipeline (Fig. 1) processes one CT series as follows; model details are given in Online Resource, Methods S1 and Table S1.
text.formatted: The pipeline (Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>) processes one CT series as follows; model details are given in Online Resource, Methods S1 and Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>.

text.text: Orientation.
Header orientation information was unreliable: the stored craniocaudal direction of all Dataset L series did not match the image content, and all Dataset HC series were stored feet first.

A small convolutional neural network classifies the craniocaudal order from coronal and sagittal mean and maximum intensity projections; the volume is reversed only if the probability of feet first exceeds 0.7, because reversing a correctly ordered volume is the more harmful error.
L1/L3 localisation.
A U-Net [20] applied to projection images outputs, for each craniocaudal position, the likelihood of being L1 or L3.
text.formatted: A U-Net <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> applied to projection images outputs, for each craniocaudal position, the likelihood of being L1 or L3.

text.text: It was trained on randomly cropped scan ranges (120 mm to the whole volume) so that it also learns the absence of a level.
A level is reported as out of range when the likelihood peak is below a threshold chosen on validation data, or when it lies within 10 mm of the first or last slice (edge rule).
Segmentation.
A two-dimensional U-Net [20] segments skeletal muscle and vertebral cortical and medullary bone on the selected slice (1 mm pixels, 512 × 512).
text.formatted: A two-dimensional U-Net <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> segments skeletal muscle and vertebral cortical and medullary bone on the selected slice (1 mm pixels, 512 × 512).

text.text: Measures.
SMA is the area of muscle pixels between -29 and 150 HU, and MSMD is their mean attenuation; the skeletal muscle index (SMI) is SMA divided by height squared.
A visceral region mask (the region enclosed by muscle, excluding muscle and vertebra) is produced.

Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) comprises pixels of -150 to -50 HU in the visceral region, and subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) pixels of -190 to -30 HU outside the visceral region and muscle; their areas and mean attenuations are computed, as are the proportion of all muscle-label pixels below -30 HU and vertebral bone attenuation.
Contrast phase.

A 2.5-dimensional ResNet18 [21] with convolutional block attention modules [22] (ct25d-regressor) classifies six phases (non-contrast, early arterial, late arterial, portal venous, venous, equilibrium) from the visceral region at L1 and L3; the class probabilities of the available levels are averaged.
text.formatted: A 2.5-dimensional ResNet18 <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> with convolutional block attention modules <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> (ct25d-regressor) classifies six phases (non-contrast, early arterial, late arterial, portal venous, venous, equilibrium) from the visceral region at L1 and L3; the class probabilities of the available levels are averaged.

text.text: Phase-0 conversion.

Each measure is converted to its non-contrast equivalent (v0) from the value in phase k (vk) with the equation of the estimated phase: a linear equation (v0 = a + b × vk) for attenuation values and proportions, and a power function (v0 = c × vkp) for SMA, VAT and SAT areas, which keeps converted areas positive.

Equations were fitted on same-examination pairs of non-contrast and phase-k series from Datasets L, O and P; for evaluation, they were refitted on the training and validation pairs only (Online Resource, Table S11).
text.formatted: Equations were fitted on same-examination pairs of non-contrast and phase-k series from Datasets L, O and P; for evaluation, they were refitted on the training and validation pairs only (Online Resource, Table <ref type="table">S11</ref>).

text.text: Age and body size.
Muscle and marrow ages at L1 and L3, height and weight are estimated with the same 2.5-dimensional network (Online Resource, Methods S2 and S4).
All analyses in this study used measured height.
Results are mapped back to the original slice order.
Examples of the output are shown in Fig. 2.
text.formatted: Examples of the output are shown in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>.

text.text: Processing one series took a median of 63 s (interquartile range 60-65 s; one graphics processing unit, including reading and writing).
All results correspond to the released version, sarco v8.6.0 (version history in Online Resource, Methods S1).
The software (sarco and ct25d-regressor) and the trained weights are publicly available (see Data availability); sarco is a research tool and has not been approved as a medical device.

The orientation classifier and the localisation models were evaluated on held-out test splits (patient-level 70/15/15 split); the orientation classifier was also evaluated on cropped scans and compared with an earlier version trained only on abdominal CT (Online Resource, Methods S1).

For truncation robustness, the test-split series of Dataset main (5-mm slices) were cut to 200 mm so that the target level was (a) in the whole, uncut scan, (b) 80-120 mm from the start of the cut, (c) 10-50 mm inside its first or last slice, (d) 5-30 mm beyond it or (e) 30-100 mm beyond it (274-303 volumes per scenario and level).

For each in-range scenario we recorded whether the level was found and whether the chosen slice was off by at least half a vertebra (16 mm, half the median vertebral height); for out-of-range scenarios, any reported level was a false detection.

Each volume was processed with the cross-fitted localisation models (see below) that had not been trained on that patient; results with the deployed models and without the edge rule are given in Online Resource, Table S12.
text.formatted: Each volume was processed with the cross-fitted localisation models (see below) that had not been trained on that patient; results with the deployed models and without the edge rule are given in Online Resource, Table <ref type="table">S12</ref>.

text.text: All datasets were also processed as they were to count series in which L1 and L3 were found.

Because the deployed segmentation and localisation models had been trained on all of Dataset main, both were retrained five times from random initialisation, each time leaving out one fold (folds stratified by cancer type and cancer-specific death), with otherwise unchanged settings.
Each series was then processed by the models that had not seen it.
Fourteen series with inconsistent reference labels were excluded, leaving 2025.

We evaluated (a) segmentation on the reference slice (Dice, SMA, MSMD) and (b) the whole pipeline with its own slice selection (slice distance, SMA, SMI, MSMD, and low muscle mass by the criteria of Fujiwara et al. [23]: L3 SMI < 36.2 cm²/m² for men and < 29.6 cm²/m² for women).

text.text: Prognosis.
In Dataset main, all predictors were taken from the cross-fitted pipeline (fully automated; missing levels treated as missing), with SMI computed from measured height.
Because the Fujiwara thresholds were derived mainly from contrast-enhanced CT, SMI was computed from areas as measured; a sensitivity analysis used phase-0 areas.
Endpoints were cancer-specific survival (CSS) and overall survival (OS) from surgery; follow-up ended in December 2022 (median 61 months; interquartile range 34-79) [4].

text.text: Two primary analyses were defined: (1) the addition of Fujiwara low muscle mass to the published baseline model (age ≥ 70 years, sex, urological cancer, stage IV) for CSS and OS (A1 vs A0); and (2) the addition of phase-0 L3 MSMD (per 10 HU) to the baseline model with body mass index (BMI) for OS (C4 vs C0).
Cox proportional hazards models were fitted, and proportional hazards were checked with Schoenfeld residuals.
Discrimination was measured by Uno's C at 60 months [27], both apparent and cross-validated (10-fold, 20 repeats, identical folds for all models).

text.text: The crossvalidated difference in C (ΔC) was the primary measure of added value; its 95% CI was obtained from 500 patient-level bootstrap samples, in each of which the whole cross-validation (10 folds, 5 repeats) was repeated.
Secondary analyses, including muscle and marrow age gaps, are described in Online Resource, Methods S3.
Values are mean ± standard deviation (SD) unless stated otherwise.
Analyses used Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.11 and statsmodels 0.15.0; Uno's C and ICCs were computed with our own implementations, which were checked against reference implementations.

text.text: Evaluated out of sample by cross-fitting, the pipeline agreed closely with radiologist-corrected labels and reproduced the prognostic associations previously reported in the same cohort.

It handled truncated scans with an accuracy similar to that on whole scans, estimated the contrast phase in short examinations, and converted contrast-enhanced attenuation to non-contrast equivalents with an error below 3 HU.
Automated L3 tools have mostly been evaluated on examinations that include L3; examinations without L3 are often excluded [7], and anatomical variants reduce the success of L3 selection [28].

text.text: Vertebral number variants also make the identity of L3 itself ambiguous, and the L3 transverse process is not a landmark independent of the segmentation pattern [29, 30]; our aim was therefore a reproducible measurement position rather than unambiguous vertebral naming.

text.text: In routine practice many examinations are short, and a tool that always returns a level will silently measure another vertebra.

Training the localiser on randomly truncated volumes kept the chosen L3 slice within half a vertebra in about 95% of in-range truncated volumes, as on whole scans, whereas TotalSegmentator, which was not designed for this task and defines the slice differently, was half a vertebra or more away in 11-14%; at L1 the two tools were closer.
The edge rule reduced false detections just outside the scan from 26-33% to 7-13%, a rate similar to TotalSegmentator, so measures from levels close to the scan end still require caution.
The much better results of the deployed models show how strongly in-sample evaluation can overstate robustness.
To our knowledge, a systematic evaluation of L3 selection on truncated scans has not been reported.
In our data, a one-slice shift had little effect on the measures whereas selecting another vertebra did, consistent with the small differences reported between slices within L3 [8, 31].

text.text: Existing corrections use a single-phase regression [10] or a phase-independent offset [14], whereas the effect of contrast differs between phases, so that fixed thresholds reclassify patients depending on the phase [32].

text.text: Estimating the phase from the image is therefore a prerequisite for phase-specific conversion.

The sarco pipeline uses only the visceral region at L1 and L3, so it works in short dynamic examinations, where TotalSegmentator, which infers the time after injection from structures from the head to the pelvis, was less accurate.

Its weakest class was the venous phase, but because phase estimation serves to select the conversion, confusion between adjacent late phases had little effect on converted attenuation (RMSE 2.81 vs 2.77 HU with the reference phase).

For areas, previous corrections used proportional equations for muscle and fat areas [10, 33] or linear regression [34], and a study of healthy donors advised against mixing contrastenhanced and non-contrast scans within a study because the contrast-related difference in visceral fat area grows with the amount of fat [35]; a power function kept converted areas positive and reduced the error for small VAT.

text.text: Phase-0 conversion matters for fixed thresholds.

The muscle attenuation thresholds used in our cohort [5] are the mean minus two standard deviations of healthy young adults on non-contrast CT [13], and their authors cautioned against applying them to contrast-enhanced CT.

text.text: Applied to the phase-0 values, they classified more than half of our older patients with cancer as low and lost much of their prognostic separation, whereas applied to the mostly portal venous values as measured, they reproduced the published prevalence (22.0% vs 21.0% [5]).

text.text: This suggests that such thresholds need validation in the target population, not that the conversion fails.
In our primary analysis, continuous phase-0 MSMD remained associated with OS in a model with BMI, but its cross-validated gain was small and uncertain (ΔC +0.012; 95% CI -0.005 to 0.024).
This study has limitations.
First, it is a single-centre study without external validation, and the scanners were mainly from two vendors.

Second, the reference labels were produced by correcting the output of an earlier version of the same model family, which may favour our pipeline over TotalSegmentator; cross-fitting removes memorisation of individual cases but not this labelling style, and no independent manual reference was created; inter-reader variability of the reference labels was not assessed.

Third, the reference phases in Datasets P and O were derived from series descriptions and protocol names without image-based verification, which may have introduced label noise, particularly for the venous phase.
Fourth, the deployed localisation models had been initialised from a model trained on all of Dataset main, so their results on Dataset main are not independent estimates.
Fifth, SMI computed from estimated height was not evaluated.

Finally, the conversion equations were derived from a limited number of paired examinations, and converted areas were uncertain when VAT was small (median overestimation 14-22% in the lowest quartile at L3 in phases 3-5; Online Resource, Table S16).
